questions.stem: In literary study, the 'transformation' of a text means:
options: referring briefly to a source so that informed readers will notice the connection
copying a source's style closely as an exercise in learning how to write
moving a source into a new medium while keeping its meaning unchanged
reworking a source in a new form, context or perspective so its meaning changes
questions.explanation: A transformation reshapes a source, and the changes produce new meaning. A brief reference is an allusion, close copying of style is imitation, and a change of medium that preserves meaning is a faithful adaptation rather than a transformation.

questions.stem: An adaptation that moves a story to a new time and place while keeping its plot is often called:
options: an abridgement
a transposition
a pastiche
an allusion
questions.explanation: Transposition relocates a story to a different setting or period. A pastiche imitates a style, an allusion is a brief reference and an abridgement shortens a text.

questions.stem: A film's opening shot lovingly recreates a famous shot from an earlier film to honour its director. This is best described as:
options: a remake
homage
parody
plagiarism
questions.explanation: Homage borrows from a source as a mark of respect. Parody mocks its target, plagiarism passes off borrowed work as one's own, and a remake retells a whole film rather than echoing one shot.

questions.stem: Parody can mock its source and pay tribute to it at the same time. Which feature of a parody best shows its affection for the original?
options: it recreates the original's style so precisely that readers recall what they loved in it
it exaggerates the original's flaws so sharply that readers notice its faults
it updates the original's setting so that modern readers can relate more easily to its story
it names the original in its title so that readers recognise the source at once
questions.explanation: Parody depends on close knowledge of its source, and skilled imitation can celebrate what it exaggerates. Sharp exaggeration of flaws is the mocking side, updating a setting is transposition, and naming a source shows recognition rather than affection.

questions.stem: A poet uses the opening line of a well-known hymn, unchanged, as the first line of a poem about a factory closure. This is best described as:
options: parody, imitating the hymn's style in order to mock its religious faith
plagiarism, since the line is reused without change or acknowledgement
appropriation, borrowing material into a new context to make new meaning
pastiche, imitating the hymn's general style without quoting its words
questions.explanation: Appropriation takes material into a new context, where it gathers new meaning: the hymn's faith now sounds against job losses. Pastiche imitates a style rather than reusing the actual words, nothing mocks the hymn, and borrowing a famous line for readers to recognise is not passing it off as one's own.

questions.stem: A student writes a paragraph closely imitating a novelist's long, comma-laden sentences. As a way of studying style, this imitation most likely helps her to:
options: produce a parody that exposes the weaknesses of the novelist's style
develop her own voice by keeping clear of other writers' influence
identify the context of production in which the novel was written
understand from the inside how the style creates its effects
questions.explanation: Writers have long learnt by imitating models, because recreating a style reveals how its rhythm and syntax work. The aim is understanding rather than mockery, imitation draws on influence rather than avoiding it, and it reveals style rather than context.

questions.stem: A reader who knows the myth of Orpheus reads a novel in which a musician loses his wife after looking back at her on a station platform. Compared with a reader who does not know the myth, she is more likely to:
options: recognise the echo and read the loss as part of an ancient pattern
read the novel as a parody that mocks the seriousness of the myth
expect the novel to end with the musician descending to the underworld
dismiss the parallel as coincidence, since novels rarely borrow from myth
questions.explanation: In the myth, Orpheus loses Eurydice when he looks back at her. Informed reading lets the allusion add depth and inevitability to the modern scene; it does not make the novel a parody, require it to retell the whole myth, or reduce the echo to coincidence.

questions.stem: Readers who choose a book labelled 'romance' expect a central love story and a satisfying ending. When such a novel ends with the heroine choosing to live alone, these expectations most likely:
options: make the ending a flaw, since a novel should follow its genre's conventions
matter little, since readers interpret an ending through their own lives
sharpen the ending's impact, prompting readers to ask why the genre's promise is refused
show that the novel has been mislabelled by its publisher and really belongs to another genre
questions.explanation: Genre conventions create expectations, and a refusal of them becomes meaningful in itself rather than a flaw or a mislabelling. The novel is still read against the romance genre, which is why the ending has force.

questions.stem: The fairy tale, once told mainly to warn children, is now often used in adult fiction to explore trauma and desire. This shows that:
options: genres can be manipulated and repurposed for new audiences and concerns
adult fiction borrows from fairy tales mainly to parody their simplicity
a genre's original purpose disappears once later writers take it over
a genre's conventions stay fixed, while its audience is free to change
questions.explanation: Conventions are challenged and changed over time: writers keep familiar fairy-tale patterns while turning them to new purposes. Parody is one possible use, not the main one shown here, and the shift depends on, rather than erases, the genre's earlier role with children.

questions.stem: A stage adaptation plays a solemn novel's dinner-party scene as comedy, and the audience laughs at lines that seemed serious on the page. Rereading the novel, a student notices its dry irony for the first time. This shows that:
options: the context of reception has changed the actual words of the novel
adaptations can reveal qualities of the original that readers had missed
the adaptation has distorted the novel by imposing humour that is not there
the director's reading has become the authoritative meaning of the novel
questions.explanation: Earlier adaptations can allow new insights into originals by drawing out features readers overlooked. The student finds the irony on the page, so the humour was not imposed; the play is one reading, not the authoritative one; and the novel's words are unchanged.

questions.stem: How can reading an imaginative adaptation help a student write an analytical essay on the original text?
options: the adaptation reveals the author's intended meaning more clearly than the text
the adaptation's changes show which parts of the original are weaknesses for her to criticise
the adaptation can be cited as a critical reading that settles the debate
the adaptation's choices act as one interpretation she can test against the original
questions.explanation: An adaptation is a reading of its source: what it keeps, cuts and changes suggests an interpretation to test against the original. It does not reveal the author's intention, mark flaws or settle the meaning.

questions.stem: Calling a sharp-eyed friend 'a real Sherlock' shows that:
options: the friend is being compared with the author of the detective stories
a literary character has become everyday shorthand for a quality
the speaker is making a learned allusion that depends on knowing the stories
the detective has been parodied, so the name now mocks his arrogance
questions.explanation: Iconic literary characters are appropriated into popular culture, where a name stands for a trait, here observant reasoning. People use the phrase without having read the stories, it praises rather than mocks, and it names the detective, not his author.

questions.stem: A shampoo advertisement shows a woman leaning from a balcony while a man calls up to her from the garden below, echoing a famous scene from a well-known play. The advertisement borrows the scene mainly to:
options: warn viewers, as the play does, about the dangers of rushing into love
attach the scene's associations of romance and longing to the product
parody the play by suggesting its romance is as shallow as an advertisement
introduce younger viewers to the play so that they will go on to read it
questions.explanation: Popular culture borrows iconic literary situations for their instant associations, which transfer to the product. The advertisement neither parodies, promotes nor moralises about the play.

questions.stem: Many people picture 'Frankenstein' as a green, bolt-necked monster, though in Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein is the scientist, and his creature is unnamed and highly articulate. This shows that popular appropriation can:
options: preserve a source's central ideas while updating its surface details
reveal the author's true intentions, which the novel itself had partly obscured
correct a source's confusing details so that it suits a modern audience
reshape and simplify a source until the popular image eclipses the original
questions.explanation: In the novel, Victor Frankenstein makes the creature, who speaks eloquently and is never named. Later films and popular culture fused the names and simplified the creature, losing its central qualities, which shows how appropriation transforms a source in the public mind rather than revealing or correcting it.

questions.stem: A poem is set to music as a song. Which transformation is most likely?
options: the singer's voice replaces the poem's speaker, so its perspective is lost
melody and a repeated chorus add emotion and change which lines carry most weight
the music illustrates the words, so the poem's meaning stays the same as before
the poem becomes a parody, since setting words to music lightens their tone
questions.explanation: A change of medium transforms a text: music adds emotional colour, and repetition in a chorus emphasises chosen lines. Meaning shifts rather than staying fixed, a musical setting need not mock or lighten a poem, and a singer voices the speaker rather than erasing the perspective.

questions.stem: A verse novel combines poetry's line breaks and white space with a novel's extended plot. Combining these forms most likely allows:
options: a sustained story told through compressed, emotionally intense moments
a story told mainly through strict rhyme and regular metre, like a ballad
a lyric meditation on a single feeling, set free of narrative and plot
a long story told through dense, detailed paragraphs of description
questions.explanation: Combining forms creates new possibilities: the novel supplies narrative scope, and poetry supplies compression and pause. Verse novels need not rhyme or follow a regular metre, they keep a novel's plot, and their white space compresses rather than expands description.

questions.stem: A novel told in letters between two lovers is rewritten as the diary of only one of them. The most significant change is that:
options: the story shifts from first-person to third-person narration, as diaries describe others
dramatic irony increases, since readers now know more than either of the lovers
the diarist becomes an unreliable narrator, since diaries are written in secret
the other lover's replies vanish, so readers get one perspective and must infer the rest
questions.explanation: The letter form gives two voices; the diary keeps one, so the other lover is seen only through the diarist's eyes. Both forms are usually first person, readers come to know less rather than more, and privacy does not make a diarist unreliable.

questions.stem: A novel is adapted as an audio drama. Which element of the novel is the adaptation most likely to convey through sound?
options: the novel's chapter divisions, through a narrator announcing each number
descriptions of setting, through ambient sounds such as gulls, wind and waves
the novel's free indirect style, through the actors' choice of accents
the narrator's descriptions of faces, through silences between the lines
questions.explanation: An audio medium replaces written description with soundscape, so setting comes through ambient sound. Accents and silences cannot carry free indirect style or facial description, and announcing chapter numbers merely reproduces the printed structure.

questions.stem: Two poems describe the same storm: in one, a farmer celebrates the rain after drought; in the other, a fisher mourns a boat lost at sea. Comparing them mainly reveals:
options: how a speaker's position shapes the representation of a single event
how rural and coastal poets use different verse forms to describe weather
how pathetic fallacy makes the storm reflect each speaker's existing mood
which speaker's response to the storm the two poets want readers to share
questions.explanation: Connected texts can represent the same event from different perspectives, and comparison exposes how position shapes meaning. Nothing is said of verse form, the storm causes each speaker's feeling rather than mirroring it, and comparison explores the difference rather than choosing a side.

questions.stem: In an original novel, the narrator mocks a vain aunt and the implied author seems to share the joke. In a later retelling, the aunt narrates, and the mockery she endures is shown as cruel. A student comparing them should conclude that:
options: the retelling's implied author takes a different stance, inviting sympathy the original withheld
the retelling's narrator must be unreliable, since she is defending herself against the original
the retelling corrects the original, proving that its implied author was simply wrong
the original's narrator and implied author differ, since the retelling exposes the cruelty
questions.explanation: Comparing perspectives of narrators and implied authors shows how the retelling revalues a character the original made comic. A later text offers a different stance rather than proving the earlier one wrong, it does not change who shares the joke within the original, and a self-defending narrator is not automatically unreliable.

questions.stem: Two connected short stories tell the same murder: one in lush, ornate sentences, the other in flat, reported statements. Which question best guides a comparison of their style?
options: Which of the two versions gives the more reliable account of the murder?
How does each story's structure build suspense about who the killer is?
What does each story reveal about its author's own attitude to violence?
How does each style shape readers' emotional distance from the crime?
questions.explanation: Comparing stylistic features means asking how each creates a different effect, here intimacy or detachment. Reliability, plot structure and the authors' attitudes are other questions, not questions of style.

questions.stem: An original novel tells its events in chronological order; a retelling tells them backwards from the ending. The retelling's structure most likely shifts readers' attention from:
options: why it happened to what happens
the characters to the plot
the narrator to the setting
what happens to why it happened
questions.explanation: When readers know the outcome from the start, suspense about events gives way to interest in causes, not the other way around. The structure changes the focus of curiosity rather than the balance of character, plot or setting.

questions.stem: A Victorian moral tale and a modern satire share the same plot of a child punished for disobedience. Comparing their purposes, the satire most likely:
options: turns the tale's lesson against itself by mocking its harshness
pays respectful homage to the tale's moral clarity and simple style
mocks modern children for disobedience the Victorians would have punished
imitates the tale as a pastiche, leaving its lesson essentially unchanged
questions.explanation: Connected texts can share a plot but differ in purpose: satire exaggerates the tale's cruelty to expose it. Homage or pastiche would leave the lesson intact, and the target is the tale's harshness, not modern children.

questions.stem: A Victorian poem pictures cheerful farm labourers singing at harvest; a modern response poem describes the same harvest through a labourer's aching back and debts. Which claim is best supported by comparing them?
options: the response parodies the original's style in order to make its readers laugh
the original is ironic, and the response simply makes that irony explicit
the original is more reliable, since it was written closer to the period
the response challenges the original's idealised, pastoral picture of rural work
questions.explanation: Comparing representations in connected texts shows how the response writes against the original's idealisation. Nothing suggests the original is ironic or the response comic, and being earlier does not make a poem more accurate.

questions.stem: A wartime speech declares 'we shall not falter'. A later poem, spoken by a mother whose son died in that war, repeats the phrase. In the poem, the phrase most likely:
options: keeps its rousing meaning, since quoted words carry their original context
becomes her private resolve to carry on, separate from the war itself
becomes ironic, questioning the cost of the resolve the speech celebrated
becomes a parody that mocks the speechmaker's voice and delivery
questions.explanation: Placed in a grieving voice, borrowed words take on new meaning: the language of resolve now sounds against loss. The poem questions the speech's purpose rather than mimicking its delivery, and the phrase's link to the war is the point.

questions.stem: Two retellings of a folk tale differ: in a 1900 version the heroine is rewarded for patient silence; in a 2020 version she is rewarded for speaking up. The difference is best explained by:
options: the values of each retelling's context shaping what the story rewards
the 2020 writer correcting an error in the 1900 writer's version
the oral tradition, in which details drift at random with each telling
each writer's personality, which matters more than the era's values
questions.explanation: Texts are influenced by their contexts, and what a retelling rewards reveals its era's values. The changes are meaningful choices, not corrections, random drift or individual quirks.

questions.stem: When comparing connected texts, which connective introduces a similarity?
options: Furthermore
Conversely
Nevertheless
Likewise
questions.explanation: 'Likewise' signals that the second point resembles the first. 'Furthermore' adds a further point without signalling likeness, while 'conversely' and 'nevertheless' introduce contrast or concession.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses comparative critical language most precisely?
options: The retelling appropriates the original by giving the servant a much larger and more important role.
The retelling is an allusion to the original, since the servant now narrates what her master once told.
Both texts explore power, but the retelling explores it far more deeply through the servant's narration.
The retelling inverts the original's power dynamic, giving the servant the narrative authority her master once held.
questions.explanation: Precise critical terms such as 'inverts' and 'narrative authority' name exactly how the texts relate. The others describe the change loosely, misuse a term, or claim more depth without saying how.

questions.stem: A student reimagines a dark adult short story about greed as a picture book for six-year-olds. Which change best keeps the story's core idea while suiting the new audience?
options: keeping the story's ideas but expressing them in the original's complex adult vocabulary
keeping the greedy character's downfall but telling it through a simple, repeated pattern and gentle humour
keeping the plot and the dark tone unchanged, but adding bright illustrations on every page
turning the greedy character into a misunderstood hero so that the ending is a happy one
questions.explanation: Reimagining for a new audience changes form and style while keeping the core idea: picture books often use repeated patterns and humour. Bright pictures do not soften an adult story's darkness, redeeming the greedy character loses the idea, and adult vocabulary does not suit the audience.

questions.stem: In a reflection on her reimagined poem, which sentence best explains the significance of a change?
options: I replaced the original's rich colour imagery with greys throughout the whole poem.
My poem's grey imagery is very effective and makes the reader feel strong emotions.
I kept the original's structure and rhyme scheme because I felt they already worked so well.
I replaced the original's rich colour imagery with greys so the city's joy feels drained.
questions.explanation: Reflecting on a manipulated aesthetic feature means naming the change and explaining its effect. Naming the change alone, claiming a vague effect or praising what was kept does not explain significance.

questions.stem: A student blends her own memory of a hospital waiting room with the sickroom setting of a classic novel to write a new scene. This mainly shows her:
options: writing pure memoir, since her own memory is the scene's real source
integrating real and imagined experience by adapting aspects of a text
transposing the novel's whole plot to a modern hospital setting
writing a parody that mocks the novel's sentimental sickroom scenes
questions.explanation: Creating new texts can mean selecting aspects of a literary text and fusing them with lived experience. She borrows one setting rather than the whole plot, nothing mocks the novel, and the novel's sickroom shapes the scene, so it is not pure memoir.
